concepts.title: AWS Global Infrastructure and the Shared Responsibility Model
concepts.description: AWS's physical infrastructure is organized into Regions and Availability Zones, and understanding that geography is what makes multi-AZ redundancy meaningful; the Shared Responsibility Model then draws the line between what AWS secures and what you must secure yourself.
learningObjectives: Explain the relationship between Regions, Availability Zones, and data centers, and why AZs are physically isolated from each other.
Explain why deploying resources across multiple AZs, not just multiple servers in one AZ, is what provides fault tolerance.
State the Shared Responsibility Model's dividing line and explain how it shifts between IaaS (EC2), managed services (RDS), and serverless (Lambda, S3).
Given a described security incident, identify whether it falls under AWS's responsibility or the customer's.
Explain why choosing a Region involves latency, compliance/data-residency, and pricing trade-offs, not just picking 'the closest one.'

sections.heading: Regions: Independent, Isolated Geographic Areas
sections.body:
An AWS Region (`us-east-1` in Northern Virginia, `eu-west-1` in Ireland, `ap-southeast-2` in Sydney, and so on) is a distinct geographic area with its own independent set of AWS infrastructure. Regions do not share data, compute, or state with each other automatically: an EC2 instance you launch in `us-east-1` does not exist, and is not even visible, when you switch your console or CLI to `ap-southeast-1`. The isolation is deliberate. It contains the blast radius: a catastrophic failure or a botched deployment in one Region cannot cascade into another the way it could if everything were one shared system. It also lets you meet data-residency requirements (GDPR rules about where EU residents' data lives, or a contract that keeps data in one country) by choosing which Region to operate in, since a Region is a commitment about where bytes are stored, not just a label.

Most AWS services are Region-scoped: you pick a Region, and everything you create with that service lives only there, addressed by ARNs that embed the Region name (S3 bucket ARNs such as `arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket` omit it because bucket names are globally unique, but the data still lives in one Region). A smaller set of services are global by design: IAM (users, roles, and policies aren't tied to any one Region), Route 53 (DNS), and CloudFront (a worldwide network of edge locations, a different and much larger concept than Regions, used to cache content close to end users). Knowing which category a service falls into matters the first time you can't find 'my resource' in the console. Usually you're looking at the wrong Region selector in the top corner. The CLI behaves the same way: it uses the Region from your profile, the `AWS_REGION` environment variable, or a `--region` flag, and a call to the wrong Region returns an empty list instead of an error, which looks exactly like 'my resources are gone'.

sections.heading: Availability Zones: Why 'Multiple Servers' Isn't the Same as 'Multiple AZs'
sections.body:
Within a Region, AWS operates multiple Availability Zones (AZs), and most Regions have three or more. Each AZ is one or more physically separate data centers with independent power, cooling, and network connectivity, typically miles apart from the other AZs in the Region. That is far enough that a single flood, fire, or power-grid failure is very unlikely to take out two AZs, and close enough that latency between AZs is low (single-digit milliseconds), so splitting a workload across AZs doesn't meaningfully hurt performance.

This trips up many people new to the cloud: launching two, three, or ten EC2 instances does not by itself buy fault tolerance against an AZ failure. If all of them live in the same AZ, they share the same power source, cooling, and network fabric, and an AZ-level event takes all of them down at once, no matter how many there are. Redundancy only protects you against the failure domain you diversify across. Two instances both in `us-east-1a` are not redundant against an AZ failure; one in `us-east-1a` and one in `us-east-1b` are, because those AZs don't share the infrastructure that is likely to fail. That is why almost every AWS reference architecture asks for at least two AZs: the AZ is the unit AWS designs as an independent failure domain. Capacity planning follows from this. With two AZs, losing one halves your capacity, so either size each AZ to carry the full load or spread across three AZs, where losing one removes only a third. Remember too that traffic between AZs is billed per GB, so multi-AZ designs have a (usually small) network cost.

sections.heading: The Shared Responsibility Model: 'Security OF the Cloud' vs 'Security IN the Cloud'
sections.body:
AWS frames its security obligations as one memorable split: AWS is responsible for the security **of** the cloud, and the customer is responsible for security **in** the cloud. 'Of the cloud' covers everything AWS owns and operates and that you can't see or control: the physical security of data centers, the durability of the underlying storage hardware, the integrity of the network backbone, and the hypervisor layer that isolates one customer's virtual machines from another's on shared physical hosts. 'In the cloud' covers everything you build on top of that: which guest-OS patches you've applied to your EC2 instances, what your application code does, whether your data is encrypted and with which keys, whether your IAM policies are correctly scoped, and whether your S3 bucket policies and security groups only allow the access you intended.

Where the line falls depends on how much of the stack a service manages for you. With EC2 (infrastructure-as-a-service), you are responsible for the guest operating system, its patches, and everything above it; AWS secures only the physical host and hypervisor. With a managed service like RDS, AWS also patches the underlying OS and the database engine, though you still own access control (IAM, security groups, database credentials) and the correctness of your data and queries. With S3 or Lambda, AWS manages nearly the whole stack, and you are left with how you configure access and what you put in it.

The distinction has practical weight. In most widely reported 'AWS data breaches', the infrastructure didn't fail. A customer left an S3 bucket publicly readable, wrote an IAM policy far broader than intended, or committed an access key to a public GitHub repo. Those sit on the 'in the cloud' side of the line, and no amount of infrastructure hardening by AWS prevents them, because they are configuration mistakes made with tools that worked as designed.

sections.heading: Choosing a Region: Latency, Compliance, and Price Are Different Axes
sections.body:
Picking 'the Region closest to me' is a reasonable default, but it is only one of several independent factors, and treating it as the only one causes problems later. Latency is the first: distance and network hops translate into round-trip time, which matters for interactive applications and much less for a nightly batch job. Compliance and data residency is a separate axis: some regulations (GDPR-related rules in the EU, data sovereignty laws in several countries) require certain data to stay in a jurisdiction, which can force a Region choice unrelated to where your team or users are. Price is a third axis: Regions are not priced identically for the same instance type or storage class, and `us-east-1`, AWS's oldest and largest Region, is often (not always) among the cheapest. The fourth is easy to forget, service availability: new AWS services and features frequently launch in `us-east-1` first and reach other Regions months later, so a Region chosen only for latency or compliance can limit which services you can use.

Everything above is about choosing *a* Region to operate in. That is a different decision from architecting for *multiple* Regions for disaster recovery, which is far more involved and expensive. Multi-AZ within one Region is the normal baseline for any production workload that cares about availability. Multi-Region is a substantial extra undertaking, because replication across Regions is neither instant nor free, and most teams reach for it only when a single Region's worst-case outage is not an acceptable business risk. Cross-Region data transfer is billed per GB, and you also have to keep configuration, secrets, and deployments consistent in two places.

examples.title: Listing a Region's Availability Zones with the AWS CLI
examples.code:
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region us-east-1 --query "AvailabilityZones[].{Name:ZoneName,Id:ZoneId,State:State}" --output table

# -------------------------------------------------
# |            DescribeAvailabilityZones           |
# +-----------+---------------+---------------------+
# |    Id     |     Name      |        State        |
# +-----------+---------------+---------------------+
# |  use1-az1 |  us-east-1a   |  available           |
# |  use1-az2 |  us-east-1b   |  available           |
# |  use1-az4 |  us-east-1d   |  available           |
# |  use1-az6 |  us-east-1f   |  available           |
# +-----------+---------------+---------------------+
examples.explanation: This lists the Availability Zones available to your account in `us-east-1`, with a stable Zone ID (`use1-az1`) next to the familiar Zone Name (`us-east-1a`). The output is abridged and account-specific: `us-east-1` has six AZs, and which ones your account sees can differ. The Zone ID is the useful part. AWS maps the letter suffixes (`a`, `b`, `c`...) to different physical AZs for different accounts, to spread load evenly instead of having everyone's first instance land in the same physical `-a` zone. So `us-east-1a` in your account is not necessarily the same data center as `us-east-1a` in someone else's. When two accounts need to confirm their subnets are in the same physical AZ (for latency, say), compare Zone IDs, not letter suffixes.

examples.title: Same Deployment, Two Different Failure Domains
examples.code:
# Single-AZ: both instances launched into the same subnet -> the same AZ
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0abcd1234 --instance-type t3.micro \
  --subnet-id subnet-aaa111 --count 2   # subnet-aaa111 lives entirely in us-east-1a

# Multi-AZ: one instance per subnet, each subnet in a different AZ
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0abcd1234 --instance-type t3.micro \
  --subnet-id subnet-aaa111 --count 1   # us-east-1a
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0abcd1234 --instance-type t3.micro \
  --subnet-id subnet-bbb222 --count 1   # us-east-1b
examples.explanation: The first block looks reasonable: two instances, presumably for redundancy. But both go into `subnet-aaa111`, and a subnet is pinned to one AZ at creation, so both end up in `us-east-1a`. If that AZ has a power or network event, both go down together. Two instances bought no protection against that failure (they would still help if one instance simply crashed). The second block launches the same capacity across two subnets in two different AZs. Now a `us-east-1a` outage leaves the `us-east-1b` instance running, because the redundancy lines up with an independent failure domain and not just a higher instance count.

examples.title: Shared Responsibility in Practice: A Public S3 Bucket
examples.explanation: Someone attached this bucket policy to `customer-exports-bucket`, probably meaning to grant read access to one application or account. `"Principal": "*"` with no `Condition` instead grants `s3:GetObject` to anyone on the internet who can guess or discover an object's key, and keys for exported customer files are the kind of thing that ends up in search indexes or leaked links. AWS is not at fault here: S3 stored every byte durably as instructed, the hardware didn't fail, and the AZ redundancy worked. The failure is in how a customer configured access to their own resource, which is the 'security in the cloud' side of the line. AWS provides S3 Block Public Access and IAM Access Analyzer as safety nets, but it does not override a policy you wrote on purpose; writing it correctly is your job.

misconceptions.description: If I launch multiple EC2 instances for my application, it's automatically fault-tolerant against infrastructure failures.
misconceptions.clarification: Fault tolerance comes from diversifying across independent failure domains, not merely from having more than one instance. If every instance lives in the same Availability Zone, they share the same power, cooling, and network, and an AZ-level event takes all of them down regardless of count. Tolerating an AZ failure takes at least two AZs (and so at least two subnets, since a subnet is pinned to one AZ), typically behind a load balancer that can route around the unhealthy AZ.
misconceptions.fact: Fault tolerance comes from diversifying across independent failure domains, not merely from having more than one instance.

misconceptions.description: Because AWS is responsible for 'security of the cloud,' AWS will notice and fix things like an overly permissive IAM policy or a publicly readable S3 bucket that I configured.
misconceptions.clarification: AWS's side of the shared responsibility line covers the physical infrastructure, hardware, network backbone, and hypervisor, not the correctness of the resources and permissions you configure on top. A misconfigured bucket policy or an overly broad IAM policy is the customer's responsibility. AWS provides IAM Access Analyzer and S3 Block Public Access to help you find and prevent these mistakes, but it does not take over getting your configuration right, and it will not override a valid policy you wrote.
misconceptions.fact: AWS's side of the shared responsibility line covers the physical infrastructure, hardware, network backbone, and hypervisor -- not the correctness of resources and permissions you configure on top of that infrastructure.

exercises.prompt: A team deployed two EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer, believing this made their service resilient to an Availability Zone outage. Below is a simplified view of the deployment. Find the reliability bug and fix it.
hints: Count how many distinct Availability Zones appear across the two instances, not how many instances there are.
The load balancer is attached to only one subnet too. That is the same underlying problem again, not a different bug.
A subnet is permanently tied to exactly one AZ, so fixing this requires introducing a second subnet that lives in a different AZ, and using it for both an instance and the load balancer.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Both instances lived in `subnet-0f1e2d3c`, which is pinned to `us-east-1a`, so despite having two instances there was one failure domain, and a `us-east-1a` outage would have taken both down. The load balancer was in the same position, attached to that one subnet. The fix moves the second instance into a new subnet, `subnet-0a9b8c7d`, in `us-east-1b`, and adds that subnet to the load balancer too. (In practice AWS requires an Application Load Balancer to have subnets in at least two AZs before it can be created, so this exact configuration could not be built as shown. The exercise is a simplified view.) Now a `us-east-1a` failure leaves the `us-east-1b` instance, and the load balancer's path to it, intact.

exercises.prompt: A company runs production EC2 instances split across three Availability Zones in one Region, behind a multi-AZ Application Load Balancer, with its data stored in S3 (which AWS replicates across multiple AZs within the Region automatically as part of the service). One Availability Zone in that Region suffers a power failure. Describe what happens to (a) the EC2 instances in the failed AZ, (b) the EC2 instances in the other two AZs, and (c) the S3 data, and explain why each behaves that way.
hints: Treat each AWS resource by asking whether it is tied to one specific AZ or spread across/managed independently of any single AZ.
The ALB continuously health-checks every registered instance -- what does it do with instances that stop responding?
S3 objects are not launched into a specific AZ the way an EC2 instance is; think about how the durability guarantee described for S3 is actually implemented.
exercises.expectedAnswer: (a) i-1, physically located in us-east-1a, becomes unreachable and effectively fails along with the rest of that AZ's power and network infrastructure. (b) i-2 and i-3, in us-east-1b and us-east-1c, are unaffected, since they run on independent power, cooling, and network infrastructure; the ALB's health checks detect that i-1 has stopped responding, mark it unhealthy, and stop routing new traffic to it, continuing to serve all traffic from i-2 and i-3. (c) The S3 data in the app-data bucket remains fully available and intact, because S3 (unlike an EC2 instance, which is launched into and stays tied to one specific AZ) stores object data redundantly across multiple AZs within the Region as an intrinsic part of how the service itself works, not as something the customer had to configure.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The scenario contrasts AZ-pinned resources with Region-scoped, AWS-managed redundancy. EC2 instances are provisioned into a subnet, and a subnet lives in one AZ, so i-1 goes down with its AZ and nothing recovers that particular instance. The ALB covers this kind of partial failure: its health checks run continuously, so once i-1 stops responding it is dropped from the routing pool after a few failed checks, and clients keep being served by the two surviving AZs at reduced capacity, not zero. S3 is a different category: you never chose an AZ when you created the bucket or wrote an object, because S3 spreads object data across multiple AZs in the Region as part of the base service (the One Zone storage classes are the exception).

assessments.prompt: A company runs a single EC2 instance in us-east-1a serving production traffic. Which change most directly improves its resilience against an Availability-Zone-level failure?
options: Resize the existing EC2 instance to a larger instance type, still in us-east-1a.
Launch a second EC2 instance in a different Availability Zone, such as us-east-1b.
Launch a second, identical EC2 instance also in us-east-1a and register both with a target group.
Migrate the instance to an entirely different AWS Region.
assessments.explanation: AZ-level fault tolerance requires diversifying across independent failure domains. Adding a second instance in the same AZ (“Launch a second, identical EC2 instance also…”) doesn't achieve that, since both instances still share the same power, cooling, and network and would fail together. Resizing to a bigger instance (“Resize the existing EC2 instance…”) addresses capacity or performance, not AZ-level failure, and leaves the single point of failure in place. Migrating Regions entirely (“Migrate the instance to an entirely different AWS Region”) is a disproportionate, much more expensive response to an AZ-level concern, and provides no redundancy either: it relocates the same single point of failure. The correct answer is the standard fix: a second instance in a different AZ, with a load balancer spanning both, so the failure of either AZ leaves the other able to serve traffic.

assessments.prompt: The AWS CLI's `describe-availability-zones` output shows both a Zone Name (like `us-east-1a`) and a Zone ID (like `use1-az1`) for each Availability Zone. Why does AWS recommend using the Zone ID rather than the Zone Name for cross-account AZ coordination?
options: Zone IDs are simply a shorter, more convenient alias for Zone Names with no functional difference between accounts.
Zone IDs are required because Zone Names only work within the AWS Management Console, not the CLI.
Zone Names are deprecated and will stop working in a future API version.

AWS deliberately maps the letter suffixes in Zone Names to different physical AZs for different accounts, to spread customer load evenly -- so 'us-east-1a' in one account may not be the same physical data center as 'us-east-1a' in another, while the Zone ID stays a stable identifier for the physical AZ.
assessments.explanation: AWS randomizes which physical AZ gets labeled 'a', 'b', 'c' per account to avoid everyone's first-launched resources piling into one physical location, so the Zone Name is account-relative, not a stable physical identifier. The Zone ID (e.g. `use1-az1`) refers to the same physical AZ in every account, which is why it is the right thing to compare when two accounts need to confirm their subnets sit in the same physical AZ (for example, to get same-AZ networking across an account boundary). The “Zone IDs are simply a shorter, more…”, “Zone Names are deprecated and will stop…”, and “Zone IDs are required because Zone Names…” options all invent reasons that don't reflect how AWS assigns these labels; Zone Names work everywhere, they're just not physically stable across accounts.

assessments.prompt: Which statement most accurately describes how the Shared Responsibility Model's dividing line shifts across EC2, RDS, and Lambda?
options: With EC2, the customer patches and secures the guest operating system and everything above it; with RDS, AWS additionally takes over OS and database-engine patching while the customer still owns access control and data; with Lambda, AWS manages nearly the entire stack and the customer is mainly responsible for their code and how they configure access to it.
The dividing line never shifts -- AWS always secures only the physical hardware and hypervisor, and the customer is always responsible for everything above that, regardless of which service is used.
With RDS, the customer is responsible for the hypervisor layer, since databases require lower-level hardware access than plain EC2 instances.
With Lambda, the customer must still patch the underlying operating system themselves, since AWS never manages OS patching for serverless compute.
assessments.explanation: The line moves with how much of the stack a service manages for you: with EC2 (infrastructure-as-a-service) AWS secures only the physical host and hypervisor and the customer owns the guest OS and up; with RDS, AWS also absorbs OS and database-engine patching, leaving the customer access control and their own data and queries; Lambda abstracts away nearly everything, leaving the customer their application code and how access to it is configured. The “The dividing line never shifts -- AWS…” option ignores that this line demonstrably does shift between service categories, and the “With Lambda, the customer must still patch…” and “With RDS, the customer is responsible…” options both invert the actual responsibility split for their respective services.

assessments.prompt: Explain the Shared Responsibility Model in your own words, including one concrete example of a security failure that would fall on AWS's side of the line, and one that would fall on the customer's side.
assessments.modelAnswer: The Shared Responsibility Model splits security obligations by who controls each layer of the stack. AWS is responsible for 'security of the cloud': the physical security of its data centers, the integrity and durability of the underlying storage and networking hardware, and the hypervisor that isolates different customers' workloads on shared machines. A customer can't see or configure any of that, so it makes no sense to hold them responsible for it. The customer is responsible for 'security in the cloud': everything they configure and build using AWS's building blocks, including which operating system patches they apply to their EC2 instances, how they write and secure their own application code, how they encrypt and handle their own data, and above all how they configure access control: IAM policies, security groups, and resource policies like S3 bucket policies. A failure on AWS's side would be, for example, a flaw in the hypervisor that let one customer's EC2 instance read another customer's memory, in infrastructure the customer never had access to and couldn't have prevented. A failure on the customer's side would be an engineer attaching a bucket policy with `"Principal": "*"` to a bucket of sensitive exports, making every object readable by anyone on the internet. S3 worked as instructed and lost nothing; the mistake was in a permission the customer controls. Most publicized cloud security incidents fall into this second category, so it pays to know where the line sits instead of assuming AWS's infrastructure security covers your own configuration mistakes.

concepts.title: IAM Fundamentals: Users, Roles, and Policies
concepts.description: IAM answers two questions on every AWS API call, who is making the request and what they are allowed to do, and understanding principals, policies, and especially roles is the foundation for using AWS safely and not just functionally.
learningObjectives: Distinguish IAM users, groups, and roles, and explain when each is the appropriate principal to use.
Read and write a basic IAM policy document, identifying Effect, Action, Resource, and Principal.
Explain why an EC2 instance or Lambda function should assume a role rather than have long-lived access keys stored on it.
Explain the principle of least privilege and why wildcards in Action or Resource are a common source of security incidents.
Trace how AWS evaluates multiple applicable policies for a single request, including the rule that an explicit Deny always overrides an Allow.

sections.heading: Principals: Users, Groups, and Roles
sections.body:
Every AWS API call is made by some **principal**, an identity IAM can recognize and evaluate permissions for. An **IAM user** is a long-lived identity meant for a specific person or application: it can have a console password, and it can have access keys (a static access key ID and secret) for programmatic access. Those credentials don't expire on their own, which makes users convenient for humans logging into the console and risky for anything else, as the next paragraph explains. A **group** is not a principal at all. It is a container you put users into so you can attach a policy once and have it apply to every member; you cannot make an API call 'as a group,' and a group can't be named as a `Principal` in a trust or resource policy. An **IAM role** has no permanent credentials of its own. A trusted principal (a human via federation, an EC2 instance, a Lambda function, another AWS account, or an AWS service) *assumes* the role through AWS's Security Token Service (STS) and receives temporary credentials, valid for anywhere from 15 minutes to 12 hours depending on configuration, which then expire automatically.

That expiry is why roles are the recommended principal for anything that isn't a human typing a password into the console. A leaked access key from a long-lived user works until someone notices and revokes it, and keys pushed to public GitHub repos are routinely scraped and abused within minutes. A leaked temporary credential is useful only for the time left before it expires, with no manual revocation needed. Also note the AWS account's **root user**: the identity created with the account, with unrestricted access to everything. IAM policies cannot restrict it (only Organizations SCPs can, in member accounts), and it should not be used for day-to-day work. AWS's guidance is to secure it with MFA, lock away its credentials, and do routine work through IAM users and roles.

sections.heading: Policies: JSON Documents That Grant or Deny
How AWS Evaluates a Request: Default Deny, and Explicit Deny Always Wins
sections.body:
Evaluation of every AWS API call follows a few fixed rules, and it is worth memorizing them because getting them backwards causes security incidents. First, everything is denied by default: an action is permitted only if some applicable policy contains an explicit `Allow` for it. Second, if *any* applicable policy (identity-based, resource-based, a permissions boundary, or an AWS Organizations Service Control Policy, SCP) contains an explicit `Deny` for that action, the request is denied, no matter how many `Allow` statements elsewhere would have permitted it. Explicit Deny always wins.

This rule is what makes permissions boundaries and SCPs useful as organization-wide guardrails: an administrator can set an SCP that denies disabling CloudTrail or using a Region, and no IAM policy written by an account admin, however broad, can override it. A permissions boundary works the same way at the level of one user or role: it sets the maximum permissions that identity-based policies can grant, and it never grants anything itself. The same rule matters in a single account. A common mistake: someone grants `s3:*` broadly to a role during development (a shortcut covered below), then tries to lock down the dangerous parts with a `Deny` on `s3:DeleteBucket`, but writes the Deny's `Resource` with a typo or an ARN pattern that doesn't match the bucket. The Deny does nothing where it was needed, and the broad Allow stays in effect. The lesson is not to avoid Deny statements. A Deny is only as good as its Resource and Action matching, and it is no substitute for not granting the broad Allow in the first place.

sections.heading: Roles for Machines: Why EC2 Instances Shouldn't Carry Access Keys
sections.body:
You can generate a long-lived IAM user access key, paste it into an EC2 instance's environment variables or a config file, and have your application authenticate that way. AWS security guidance consistently flags this as an anti-pattern: the key is a static secret on disk that never expires, and every place such a secret sits is another place it can leak, whether committed to a repo by accident, baked into an AMI, printed by a log line, or stolen if the instance is compromised.

The standard alternative is an **IAM role attached to the instance via an instance profile**. The EC2 Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) on the instance then serves rotating temporary credentials to any AWS SDK or CLI call made from it, so no access key is ever generated, stored, or handled by a person. Prefer IMDSv2, which requires a session token for each metadata request and blocks the simple SSRF attacks that can read IMDSv1 credentials; you can require it at launch with `--metadata-options HttpTokens=required`. To see which identity your CLI or code is using, run `aws sts get-caller-identity`; it is the quickest check when a call fails with AccessDenied. The same pattern applies to a Lambda function's **execution role** and an ECS task's **task role**: the compute resource assumes a role and gets short-lived credentials scoped to that role's policy, refreshed automatically. This removes a whole category of risk, since there is no static secret for an attacker, or a bot scraping public repositories for `AKIA...` access keys, to find.

sections.heading: Least Privilege, and the Trouble With Wildcards
sections.body:
The **principle of least privilege** says a policy should grant the actions and resources a principal needs to do its job, and nothing more. It's routinely violated for an understandable reason: while building something new, nobody wants to work out the minimal permission set, so people reach for `"Action": "s3:*"` or even `"Action": "*", "Resource": "*"` to get unblocked, with a mental note to tighten it later that in many codebases never happens before production.

The risk is practical. A role with `s3:*` on `Resource: *` can do more than read the one bucket the application needs: it can delete objects, delete buckets, and rewrite bucket policies on *every* bucket in the account, including ones unrelated to the application. If its credentials are misused (through a compromised dependency, an SSRF bug, or any other route into the application), the blast radius is the account's whole S3 footprint. The discipline that avoids this is to start narrow, granting the specific actions on the specific resources you know you need, and to expand as CloudTrail logs or IAM Access Advisor reveal permissions you missed, instead of starting broad and hoping someone narrows it later. The IAM policy simulator and the policy validation in Access Analyzer let you test a policy before you attach it. IAM Access Analyzer can help surface policies broader than their actual usage.

examples.title: A Least-Privilege S3 Policy vs. an Overly Broad One
examples.explanation: The narrow policy's `Resource` matches only objects inside `app-data-bucket`: the `/*` suffix means 'any object key in this bucket', not the bucket itself. A principal with only this policy can read objects from that one bucket and do nothing else in S3: no deleting, no listing, no touching other buckets. The broad policy looks similar at a glance, but `"s3:*"` on `"Resource": "*"` grants every S3 action (`GetObject`, `PutObject`, `DeleteObject`, `DeleteBucket`, `PutBucketPolicy`, and dozens more) against every bucket that exists or will exist in the account. Attach it to the role of a single reporting microservice, and that service's leaked credentials become a master key to every bucket in the account.

examples.title: An EC2 Instance Role's Trust Policy vs. Its Permissions Policy
examples.explanation: These are two different documents that are easy to conflate. The trust policy says which principal may call `sts:AssumeRole` on this role, here the EC2 service, which is what lets you attach the role to an instance through an instance profile. Change the `Principal` to `lambda.amazonaws.com` and a Lambda function could assume the same role; change it to another AWS account's ARN and that account could (a common cross-account pattern). The permissions policy answers a separate question: once something has assumed the role, what may it do? Here, read and write objects in one bucket. A common beginner confusion is to think that broadening the trust policy grants more permissions, or that the permissions policy controls who can use the role.

examples.title: An Explicit Deny Overriding a Broad Allow
examples.explanation: Both policies are attached to the same role and evaluated together for every request it makes. Policy A's `s3:*` on `Resource: *` would alone allow `DeleteBucket` along with everything else in S3. Policy B explicitly denies `s3:DeleteBucket` on all resources. An explicit Deny overrides any Allow regardless of which policy it is in or the order of attachment, so the role can do anything `s3:*` allows except delete a bucket. A broad Allow plus a narrow Deny as a guardrail is a legitimate technique, but as noted earlier it is only as reliable as the Deny's Action and Resource matching: a typo or too-narrow ARN would leave the broad Allow exposed for whatever the Deny missed.

misconceptions.description: IAM groups are a kind of principal, so you can write a policy's Principal field as a group, or a role can effectively 'be' a group.
misconceptions.clarification: A group is an administrative container for attaching policies to many users at once. It is not a principal: it can't make API calls, be assumed, or be named in the `Principal` field of a trust or resource policy. Only users, roles, AWS services, and AWS accounts act as principals. To share permissions between different kinds of callers (a human and an EC2 instance, say), attach the same policy to each principal (a user and a role) individually. Groups only help when many IAM users need the same identity-based policy.

misconceptions.description: As long as a policy statement has Effect: Allow for a given action, that action is permitted.
misconceptions.clarification: An Allow only takes effect if there is no applicable explicit Deny anywhere else in scope: the principal's own identity-based policies, any relevant resource-based policy, any permissions boundary, and any AWS Organizations Service Control Policy. Because everything is denied by default and an explicit Deny overrides any Allow wherever it is defined, a seemingly sufficient Allow can still end in access denied if another applicable policy denies the same action or resource.
misconceptions.fact: An Allow only takes effect if there is no applicable explicit Deny anywhere else in scope -- across the principal's own identity-based policies, any relevant resource-based policy, any permissions boundary, and any AWS Organizations Service Control Policy.

exercises.prompt: A developer wrote this policy intending to let an application role read objects only from the 'reports-bucket' S3 bucket. A security review found the role can actually read from every bucket in the account. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Look at the Resource field: what set of ARNs does the string it holds match?
An S3 object ARN has the shape arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/key-name. What ARN pattern would match only objects inside reports-bucket, and nothing else?

Remember that the bucket's own ARN (arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket) and the objects inside it (arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/*) are different resources -- GetObject acts on the object-level ARN, which needs the /* suffix.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original `"Resource": "*"` matches every resource ARN, across every service and every bucket in the account, not just one bucket's objects. The fix scopes it to `arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/*`, which matches only object keys in reports-bucket. A companion mistake often follows: if the role also needs `s3:ListBucket` (to enumerate the bucket rather than read a known object), that action applies to the bucket ARN without `/*`, because listing is an operation on the bucket itself. It needs a second statement with `"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket"`, and forgetting it is a common follow-up bug.

exercises.prompt: Write a least-privilege identity-based IAM policy (JSON) that allows a role to read and write objects, but never delete them, and only within the 'uploads/' prefix of a bucket named 'user-uploads-bucket'. The role should not be able to do anything else.
hints: Which two S3 action names correspond to reading and writing an object? Since delete should never be permitted, does the policy need a Deny for it, or can it omit that action from the Allow?
The Resource ARN needs to express 'any object key under the uploads/ prefix inside user-uploads-bucket' -- think about where the wildcard needs to go relative to the prefix.
Double-check scope: the exercise only asks for object-level get/put access under a prefix, not bucket-level actions like ListBucket -- don't grant permissions beyond what was actually asked for.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The `Action` array lists only `s3:GetObject` and `s3:PutObject`. Leaving out `s3:DeleteObject` satisfies 'never delete' more robustly than granting it and cancelling it with a Deny, because an action that was never allowed can't be re-enabled by a mismatched or missing Deny elsewhere. (Another policy attached to the same role could still allow delete, so this is least privilege for this policy, not a guarantee for the role.) The `Resource` ARN, `arn:aws:s3:::user-uploads-bucket/uploads/*`, matches only keys beginning with `uploads/` in that bucket, so an object like `exports/report.csv` is out of scope. The policy omits `s3:ListBucket` because it is a bucket-level action (it would need the bare bucket ARN, `arn:aws:s3:::user-uploads-bucket`) and the exercise asked only for get/put on objects under a prefix. Least privilege means resisting 'while I'm at it' permissions nobody requested.

assessments.prompt: An engineer attaches two policies to the same IAM role: Policy A allows `s3:*` on `Resource: *`. Policy B explicitly denies `s3:DeleteObject` on `Resource: *`. What can the role actually do?
options: Only DeleteObject is blocked temporarily until an administrator manually resolves the conflict between the two policies attached to the role.
Everything s3:* allows, including DeleteObject, because Policy A was attached first.
Everything s3:* allows except DeleteObject, because an explicit Deny always overrides an Allow regardless of attachment order.
Nothing at all, because the two conflicting policies cancel each other out entirely.
assessments.explanation: IAM policy evaluation applies the rule that an explicit Deny overrides any Allow for the same action and resource, whichever policy document it is in and in whatever order policies were attached, so attachment order does not matter (“Everything s3:* allows, including DeleteObject, because Policy…”), policies do not 'cancel out' into total denial (the “Nothing at all, because the two conflicting…” option, which would also block every other s3 action the role needs), and no manual resolution step is needed at evaluation time (the “Only DeleteObject is blocked temporarily until…” option: the Deny wins on every request, immediately). The role keeps every permission s3:* grants except DeleteObject, which the explicit Deny blocks.

assessments.prompt: An IAM role's trust policy currently has `{ "Principal": { "Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" }`. A team now wants a Lambda function, instead of an EC2 instance, to be able to assume this same role and use its existing permissions policy unchanged. What must they change?
options: Nothing -- any AWS service can assume any role automatically, regardless of what its trust policy's Principal says.
The role's permissions policy, by adding `lambda:InvokeFunction` to its Action list.
The role's trust policy, updating its Principal to include `lambda.amazonaws.com`.
Nothing can be changed -- a role's trust policy is permanently fixed to whichever service it was originally created for.
assessments.explanation: The trust policy says who may assume the role, and the permissions policy says what the role can do once assumed. The desired permissions are already correct, so only the trust policy's Principal needs updating, to include the Lambda service. The “Nothing -- any AWS service can assume…” option is wrong because AssumeRole is gated by the trust policy, not granted universally; the “The role's permissions policy, by adding `lambda:InvokeFunction`…” option confuses the permissions policy with the trust policy; the “Nothing can be changed -- a role's…” option is wrong because trust policies are ordinary, editable IAM documents, not permanently fixed at creation.

assessments.prompt: A team wants an IAM user (used by a developer) and an IAM role (assumed by an EC2 instance) to share an identical set of permissions, and considers creating an IAM group that both the user and the role could join. What is the problem with this plan?
options: The plan works, but only for roles attached to EC2 instances specifically, not Lambda functions.

A group is not itself a principal and cannot be assumed or referenced as a Principal, and a role cannot be placed into a group at all -- the correct approach is to attach the same policy document directly to both the user and the role.
Nothing -- IAM groups can contain both users and roles, so adding both to the same group is a standard way to share permissions.
Groups can only be used with resource-based policies, not identity-based policies, so this plan would need a bucket policy instead.
assessments.explanation: A group is an administrative container for attaching a policy to many IAM users at once. It is not a principal, cannot be assumed via sts:AssumeRole, cannot appear in a Principal field, and roles cannot be added to groups at all (only users can be members). Identical permissions for a user and a role require attaching the same policy to each individually. The “The plan works, but only for roles…” option invents a distinction between EC2 and Lambda roles that doesn't exist for this purpose, and the “Groups can only be used with resource-based…” option misdescribes what groups can be used with -- they only ever affect identity-based policy attachment for users, never resource-based policies.

assessments.prompt: A new engineer on your team wants to give a Lambda function access to AWS resources by generating an IAM user access key and storing it as an environment variable in the function's configuration. Explain why this is generally the wrong approach and what to do instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: The problem is that an IAM user's access key is a static, long-lived secret that doesn't expire. Once it sits in the Lambda function's environment configuration, someone has to rotate it and revoke it by hand if it is compromised, and every place a static secret is stored is another chance to leak: a log line, an overly permissive policy on who can read the function's configuration, or a copy pasted into a script that later gets committed. The correct approach is to give the Lambda function an execution role instead: attach an IAM role to the function, write a permissions policy on that role scoped to exactly what the function needs (following least privilege, not a broad grant), and let Lambda's own infrastructure handle assuming that role and injecting short-lived, automatically-rotating temporary credentials into the function's runtime environment via AWS's Security Token Service. The AWS SDK inside a Lambda function discovers and uses these temporary credentials with no code changes, so there is no access key to generate, store, or rotate, and exposed credentials would expire soon instead of staying valid indefinitely. EC2 instance roles and ECS task roles follow the same pattern: compute that needs AWS access should assume a role, not carry a user's static credentials.

assessments.prompt: A developer asks you to attach the AdministratorAccess policy to a Lambda function's role 'just to get it working' because it keeps failing with AccessDenied when writing to one S3 bucket. What do you do instead, and why?
assessments.modelAnswer: Granting admin to fix one missing permission violates least privilege: if the function is ever compromised or buggy, it could delete anything in the account. Instead read the AccessDenied message or CloudTrail event to see the exact action and resource that was denied, for example s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/*. Add a narrowly scoped policy to the role allowing only that action on that bucket prefix. Check the other side too: a bucket policy, KMS key policy or SCP can also deny the call even when the role allows it, so verify each layer. Use the IAM policy simulator or Access Analyzer to confirm, keep policies in infrastructure as code so they are reviewed, and explain to the developer that a precise policy is a one-line change that removes a large blast radius.

concepts.title: EC2 and Instance Types
concepts.description: EC2 rents virtual machines by instance type and by the second, and picking the right family and size means matching your workload's bottleneck (CPU, memory, network, or burst pattern) to what you pay for, not just picking bigger.
learningObjectives: Explain what EC2 provides (a virtualized, isolated slice of physical hardware) and how that differs from provisioning an on-premises server.
Decode an instance type name (e.g. m6g.xlarge, c6i.2xlarge) into its family, generation, capability flags, and size.
Match an instance family to a workload profile (compute-bound, memory-bound, burstable, network-intensive).
Explain burstable (t-family) CPU credits and why a sustained high-CPU workload on a t-family instance is a common performance and cost trap.
Distinguish On-Demand, Reserved/Savings Plans, and Spot pricing models and identify which is appropriate for a given workload.

sections.heading: What EC2 Actually Gives You
sections.body:
EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) provides virtual machines running on top of AWS's own hypervisor (the Nitro System, on current-generation instances): when you launch an instance, you get an isolated slice of a physical host's CPU cores, memory, and network bandwidth, kept separate from other customers' instances on the same hardware. The difference from an on-premises server is less the hardware than the economics and elasticity around it: there is no procurement lead time (an instance is typically running within a minute or so of the launch call), you pay per second or per hour only while it runs, and when you terminate it you stop paying, with no depreciating asset left in a rack. The billing detail to remember: stopping an EBS-backed instance ends the compute charge but its EBS volumes keep billing, and terminating deletes the root volume by default (the `DeleteOnTermination` setting) while additional volumes are kept unless configured otherwise.

One detail surprises people from a traditional server background: an EC2 instance's root volume is usually backed by EBS (Elastic Block Store), a separate network-attached block storage service, not part of the same host as the compute. That is what lets an instance be stopped and later started on a different physical host with its volume intact. EBS is a different service from S3 (covered below): EBS behaves like an attached disk with a filesystem, and S3 does not.

sections.heading: Decoding an Instance Type Name
sections.body:
An instance type name like `m6g.xlarge` or `c6i.2xlarge` packs several pieces of information into a short string, and reading it fluently is useful day to day. The leading letter is the **family**, which signals the intended workload profile: `m` (general purpose, a balanced ratio of CPU to memory), `c` (compute optimized, more CPU per dollar, less memory), `r` (memory optimized, more RAM per dollar, less relative CPU), `t` (burstable general purpose, covered in detail below), and `g`/`p` (GPU-accelerated, for ML training/inference or graphics workloads). The number after the family letter is the **generation**: `6` is newer than `5` in the same family, generally with better price-performance, and it's usually worth using the newest available unless something (like software certified only for an older generation) argues otherwise. Extra lowercase letters after the generation are **capability flags**: `g` means the instance uses AWS's own Graviton (ARM-based) processor instead of an x86 chip (`i` is Intel, `a` is AMD). Graviton instances are often cheaper and more power-efficient, but your software must run on ARM, either natively or through multi-architecture container images. Finally, the part after the dot is the **size** (`nano`, `micro`, `small`, `medium`, `large`, `xlarge`, `2xlarge`, ...), where each step up roughly doubles vCPU count and memory versus the previous size within the same family.

Family choice should follow your bottleneck, not habit or a guess. A batch video-transcoding job that pegs every CPU core is compute-bound and belongs on a `c`-family instance. An in-memory cache or database that is constantly short of RAM but not CPU belongs on an `r`-family instance; a bigger `c`-family instance would add CPU it doesn't need and barely raise the memory ceiling. A web server with low average load and occasional short bursts can fit the cheaper `t`-family, with the caveat covered next.

sections.heading: Burstable Instances and CPU Credits: The t-family Gotcha
sections.body:
`t`-family instances (`t3`, `t3a`, `t4g`, and so on) are priced on the assumption that most workloads sit well below full CPU most of the time, with occasional short spikes. Each `t`-family instance has a **baseline performance** level per vCPU and continuously earns **CPU credits** while running below it; it spends credits to burst above baseline. As long as bursts are occasional and brief, the accrued balance absorbs them and you get burst-capable performance at a fraction of the cost of a fixed-performance instance sized for peak load.

The trap appears when load isn't occasional. A workload running high CPU for hours burns through its credit balance faster than it is replenished, and once the balance is zero, behavior depends on the instance's **credit mode**. In 'standard' mode the CPU is throttled back to the (much lower) baseline, producing a performance cliff that looks like the instance 'suddenly got slow' with no code change. In 'unlimited' mode the instance keeps performing above baseline but incurs additional charges for the extra CPU, so you get a bill spike instead of a cliff. The default depends on the generation: T2 launches in standard mode, while T3, T3a, and T4g launch in unlimited mode. To do the arithmetic: 1 credit is one vCPU at 100% for one minute, a `t3.micro` has 2 vCPUs and earns 12 credits per hour, so its baseline is 12 / 60 / 2 = 10% per vCPU. Either way, `t`-family instances suit spiky, mostly idle workloads and are a poor fit for sustained high load, which belongs on a fixed-performance family (`m`, `c`, or `r`, depending on the bottleneck).

sections.heading: Pricing Models: On-Demand, Reserved/Savings Plans, and Spot
sections.body: The same instance type can be bought under different commitment models, and the right one depends on how predictable and how interruption-tolerant the workload is. **On-Demand** has no commitment: you pay a per-second or per-hour rate only while the instance runs. It has the highest hourly rate of the three and is the right default for anything unpredictable, short-lived, or still being sized, since you aren't locking in a wrong guess. **Reserved Instances** and **Savings Plans** (the more flexible alternative) commit you to a 1-year or 3-year term in exchange for a substantial discount, up to roughly 70% off On-Demand for the longest commitments. They suit a workload you know will run continuously for the term, such as a baseline production fleet, not one you are still validating. **Spot Instances** are AWS's spare capacity, at the current Spot price and often 70-90% off On-Demand, with the catch that AWS can reclaim the capacity with a two-minute interruption notice when it needs it back. Spot fits stateless, checkpointable, or cheaply retryable work: batch processing, CI/CD runners, rendering, or a stateless web fleet that can lose any instance without users noticing. It is a bad fit for anything stateful that can't survive sudden termination, like a single unreplicated database. To reduce interruptions, request several instance types across several AZs (an Auto Scaling group with a mixed instances policy does this), so a capacity shortage in one pool doesn't take out the whole fleet.

sections.heading: AMIs: The Template an Instance Launches From
sections.body:
Every EC2 instance launches from an **AMI** (Amazon Machine Image), a template that bundles a root volume snapshot with launch metadata such as the architecture it supports. AWS publishes maintained AMIs for common operating systems (Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, Windows Server), the AWS Marketplace offers vendor AMIs, and you can bake a **custom AMI**: install your application and dependencies on a running instance, then create an AMI from its current state. AMIs belong to one Region, so to launch from one in another Region you copy it there first (`aws ec2 copy-image`). To check what an instance type gives you before choosing, `aws ec2 describe-instance-types --instance-types m6g.xlarge --query "InstanceTypes[0].[VCpuInfo.DefaultVCpus,MemoryInfo.SizeInMiB]"` prints its vCPU count and memory.

A custom AMI pays off once you have more than a handful of instances, especially with autoscaling (covered in a later concept). If new instances launch from a generic base AMI and run a long bootstrap script on every boot, scaling out under sudden load is slow, and a transient failure partway through the script leaves a half-configured instance. With everything pre-installed in the AMI, a new instance is ready almost as soon as it boots, with faster and more reliable launches than a from-scratch script at scale. That is why 'golden AMI' pipelines, which rebuild and publish an AMI on every application release, are standard in mature AWS deployments.

examples.title: Decoding Three Instance Type Names Against Their Likely Workloads
examples.code:
m6g.xlarge   -> m = general purpose, 6 = 6th gen, g = Graviton (ARM), xlarge size
             -> balanced CPU/memory; good default for a typical web/app server

c6i.2xlarge  -> c = compute optimized, 6 = 6th gen, i = Intel, 2xlarge size
             -> CPU-heavy ratio; good for video encoding, batch computation, CI build fleets

r5.large     -> r = memory optimized, 5 = 5th gen, (no extra flag = x86, non-Graviton), large size
             -> high RAM-to-CPU ratio; good for in-memory caches, large in-memory databases
examples.explanation: Each name maps onto a workload decision. `m6g.xlarge` is a balanced default when you don't yet know your bottleneck (a new service in early development), and the `g` flag makes it one of the cheaper options per vCPU if your software runs on ARM. `c6i.2xlarge` trades relative memory for more CPU per dollar, which pays off only for CPU-bound work: a memory-bound workload here wastes money on idle CPU while the memory constraint barely improves. `r5.large` is the mirror image, with more memory per dollar and less relative CPU, suited to something like an in-memory cache where CPU use is low and dataset size in RAM determines performance. Let CloudWatch metrics under real load show which resource is saturated, instead of defaulting to whichever size 'sounds about right.'

examples.title: Launching an Instance Tied to a Specific AZ and IAM Role
examples.code:
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0abcdef1234567890 \
  --instance-type m6g.large \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=app-server-role \
  --subnet-id subnet-0f1e2d3c \
  --security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --count 1
examples.explanation: This command pulls together several earlier ideas. `--image-id` names the AMI the instance boots from; a custom AMI comes up with the application already installed. `--instance-type m6g.large` picks a balanced Graviton-based type for a general-purpose app server, so the AMI must be an arm64 image. `--subnet-id subnet-0f1e2d3c` pins the instance to the one AZ that subnet belongs to, so a second instance for redundancy needs a different subnet in a different AZ. `--iam-instance-profile Name=app-server-role` attaches an IAM role instead of embedding an access key, so SDK calls on the instance authenticate with temporary credentials served by the instance metadata service. The AMI ID and resource IDs are placeholders.

examples.title: The Burstable-Instance Trap: Watching CPU Credits Run Out
examples.code:
time      CPUUtilization   CPUCreditBalance   note
09:00     15%               144                idle-ish, earning credits
09:15     20%               150                still earning
09:30     85%               140                burst begins, spending credits
10:00     85%                60                sustained burst, balance dropping fast
10:30     85%                 0                balance exhausted
10:31     22%                 2                THROTTLED to baseline -- utilization capped, NOT by demand
examples.explanation: The numbers are illustrative, not computed for a specific instance size, and the instance is assumed to be in standard credit mode. CPUUtilization alone looks like a normal, if elevated, load pattern. CPUCreditBalance tells the story: the instance accrued credits while below baseline, then at 09:30 a sustained load pushed it well above baseline and it spent credits faster than it earned them. By 10:30 the balance is zero, and at 10:31 CPUUtilization drops to 22%, not because demand dropped but because the instance is throttled to baseline and can't deliver more CPU however much load is waiting. To the application this looks like an unexplained cliff. To the infrastructure it is the predictable result of running sustained load on a family designed for short bursts.

misconceptions.description: If you're not sure what instance type you need, picking a bigger and more expensive one is always the safe choice.
misconceptions.clarification: 'Bigger' only helps if it adds capacity in the dimension that is bottlenecked. Moving a CPU-bound encoding job to a larger memory-optimized instance adds RAM it was never short of while the CPU constraint barely changes. Right-sizing means looking at CloudWatch metrics (CPU, memory via the CloudWatch agent, network, disk) to find the saturated resource, then choosing a family that targets it, instead of using 'bigger' as a substitute for diagnosing the bottleneck.

misconceptions.description: Spot Instances are just a cheaper version of On-Demand with no meaningful downside besides the discount.
misconceptions.clarification: Spot Instances can be reclaimed by AWS with a two-minute interruption notice whenever AWS needs the capacity back, which is a different reliability contract from On-Demand, not just a pricing difference. Spot suits workloads that are stateless, checkpointable, or cheaply retryable (batch jobs, CI runners, stateless fleets) and is a poor fit for anything stateful or latency-sensitive that can't absorb sudden termination.

exercises.prompt: A t3.micro instance in standard credit mode runs sustained CPU load at 80% utilization for several hours straight, well above its baseline. Given what you know about CPU credits, predict what happens to its performance over that period, and why.
exercises.code:
credit_mode: standard
baseline_performance_pct: 10   # t3.micro: 10% per vCPU, as CloudWatch reports it
starting_credit_balance: 144   # accrued (t3.micro can accrue at most 288)
observed_utilization: 80%  (sustained for hours)
hints: Is this instance earning credits or spending them while running at 80%, given that its baseline is only 10%?
A finite starting balance being spent faster than it's replenished will eventually reach zero -- what does 'standard' credit mode do at that point?
Think about what happens to CPUUtilization itself, not just the credit balance, once the balance hits zero in standard mode.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The instance spends credits continuously (80% is far above the 10% baseline), draining the balance of 144 in under two hours: at 80% on 2 vCPUs it spends 96 credits per hour and earns 12, a net loss of 84 per hour. At zero, standard mode throttles the CPU to the 10% baseline, so CPUUtilization drops sharply, not because load decreased but because the instance can't deliver more, producing a sudden performance degradation with no drop in demand.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Running at 80% against a 10% baseline means credits are spent every minute with no offsetting accumulation (1 credit is one vCPU at 100% for one minute, so 2 vCPUs at 80% spend 96 credits per hour against 12 earned). The 144-credit balance therefore depletes in roughly 1.7 hours. Once it reaches zero, standard mode enforces the baseline as a hard ceiling, and the instance is throttled to about 10% utilization however much demand is waiting. On a dashboard, utilization appears to fall although the incoming load hasn't changed. The fix is either unlimited credit mode (accepting extra charges to sustain the burst; this is the default on T3) or, if the load is sustained, moving to a fixed-performance family sized for the real load.

exercises.prompt: A team runs an in-memory caching layer (similar to Redis) on a c5.xlarge instance. They keep seeing frequent evictions and out-of-memory errors even though CPUUtilization stays consistently low. Diagnose the instance-type bug and propose a fix.
exercises.code:
instance_type: c5.xlarge     # compute optimized, 4 vCPU / 8 GiB RAM
workload: in-memory-cache
observed_cpu_utilization: 12%
observed_symptom: frequent evictions, occasional OOM errors
hints: Low CPU utilization alongside memory pressure is a strong signal about which resource is actually the bottleneck here.
The c-family is compute optimized because it trades relative memory for more CPU. Is that a good match for a workload whose job is holding data in RAM?
Look for a family optimized for a high memory-to-CPU ratio, at a comparable size, rather than moving to a bigger instance in the same family.
exercises.solutionCode:
instance_type: r5.xlarge      # memory optimized, 4 vCPU / 32 GiB RAM
workload: in-memory-cache
# same vCPU count as before, ~4x the RAM -- targets the actual bottleneck directly
exercises.solutionExplanation: 12% CPU alongside frequent evictions and OOM errors is a memory bottleneck, not a compute one: the instance runs out of RAM for the cache's working set long before it runs short of CPU. The c5.xlarge is compute optimized, so its 8 GiB of RAM is modest relative to its CPU, which is backwards for a workload whose purpose is holding data in memory. Switching to r5.xlarge keeps the same 4 vCPUs but quadruples RAM to 32 GiB, targeting the constrained resource. Moving to a bigger c-family instance (c5.2xlarge) would buy CPU the workload doesn't need while only doubling memory to 16 GiB.

assessments.prompt: A nightly batch job compresses large video files and finishes faster with more CPU cores available, but its memory usage stays low and predictable throughout. Which instance family is the most appropriate choice?
options: A c-family (compute optimized) instance, to maximize CPU throughput per dollar for this CPU-bound workload.
An r-family (memory optimized) instance, to comfortably hold each file in memory during processing.
A t-family (burstable) instance, since the job only runs briefly once per night.
The cheapest available instance type regardless of family, since batch jobs are not latency-sensitive, so any will do.
assessments.explanation: The workload is CPU-bound (it finishes faster with more cores) with low, predictable memory use, which is the profile a compute-optimized c-family instance targets: maximum CPU per dollar without paying for unused memory (which rules out the “An r-family (memory optimized) instance, to comfortably…” option). The “A t-family (burstable) instance, since the job…” option is a trap: 'runs briefly once per night' sounds like burstable pricing, but a batch job holding high CPU for its whole run is the sustained-load pattern that exhausts t-family credits and triggers throttling (or extra charges in unlimited mode). Short but at full intensity is not the same as mostly idle. The “The cheapest available instance type regardless…” option ignores the workload profile; the cheapest type is a good choice only if it matches the bottleneck, which for a CPU-bound job is what the c-family is built for.

assessments.prompt: A team is considering switching their fleet from c6i.2xlarge to c6g.2xlarge to reduce cost. What must be true for this migration to work correctly?
options: Graviton instances only run Windows Server, so this migration only matters if the fleet currently runs Windows.
They must move up to a larger size, such as 4xlarge, to compensate for a slower clock speed on Graviton hardware.
Nothing needs to change -- the letters after the generation number are purely cosmetic and never affect compatibility.
Their application (or its container images) must support the ARM architecture.
assessments.explanation: The lowercase letters after the generation number are capability flags: 'g' means the instance runs on AWS's Graviton (ARM) processor instead of an x86 chip like the 'i' (Intel) variant. ARM and x86 are different instruction set architectures, so software or container images built only for x86 won't run unmodified on Graviton. The migration is safe only once the application is confirmed to run on ARM, natively or via multi-architecture images. Note also that an AMI is built for one architecture, so the team needs an arm64 AMI, and for containers a multi-architecture image built with something like `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64`. The “Nothing needs to change -- the letters…” option misreads capability flags as meaningless, the “They must move up to a larger…” option invents a clock-speed compensation requirement, and the “Graviton instances only run Windows Server…” option fabricates an OS restriction. The real constraint is architecture compatibility, not the operating system.

assessments.prompt: Two teams each run a t3.medium instance that occasionally exceeds its baseline CPU performance. Team A's instance uses 'standard' credit mode; Team B's uses 'unlimited' credit mode. Both instances exhaust their CPU credit balance during a sustained traffic spike. What happens to each?
options: Team A's instance is throttled down to its baseline performance level; Team B's instance keeps performing above baseline but starts incurring additional charges for the extra CPU usage beyond what its credits covered.

Both instances are throttled identically back to baseline performance, since credit mode only changes how fast credits are earned, not what happens when they run out, so both teams see the same performance and neither team is billed for any additional usage.
Both instances continue performing above baseline indefinitely at no extra charge, because credit balances regenerate instantly once they hit zero.
Team A's instance is automatically terminated when its credit balance reaches zero; Team B's instance is throttled instead.
assessments.explanation: Credit mode governs what happens once the balance is exhausted. In standard mode the CPU is throttled back to baseline, so Team A's instance slows down however much demand remains. In unlimited mode the instance keeps bursting above baseline with a zero balance, spending surplus credits, and AWS bills for the average usage above baseline instead of throttling, so Team B's instance keeps performing and the bill reflects the overage. The “Both instances are throttled identically back…” option collapses this distinction, the “Team A's instance is automatically terminated…” option invents a termination behavior that credit exhaustion doesn't cause, and the “Both instances continue performing above baseline indefinitely…” option ignores that credits are finite and replenished gradually.

assessments.prompt: Explain how you would decide between On-Demand, Reserved Instances/Savings Plans, and Spot Instances for three different workloads: a steady-state production API fleet that runs 24/7 year-round, a nightly data-processing batch job that can be retried if interrupted, and a brand-new service whose traffic pattern isn't well understood yet.
assessments.modelAnswer: The pricing model follows from how predictable and how interruption-tolerant each workload is, not from which is cheapest in isolation. The steady-state production API fleet running 24/7 is the case Reserved Instances or Savings Plans are built for: you know this capacity will run for at least a year, so committing captures a substantial discount (up to around 70% off On-Demand) on capacity you would pay for anyway, with no uncertainty being locked in. The nightly batch job is the classic Spot candidate: it is retryable, so an interruption (with a two-minute notice when AWS reclaims capacity) means a retry and not an incident, and the 70-90% discount is worth that risk for work that isn't user-facing or time-critical. Checkpointing progress to S3 or a queue means a replacement instance resumes where the interrupted one stopped. The brand-new service with unknown traffic should start On-Demand: a 1- or 3-year commitment before you know the steady-state capacity risks locking in the wrong count or type, and On-Demand lets you observe real usage and right-size first. Mature accounts usually run a blend: a Reserved or Savings Plan baseline sized to known load, with On-Demand or Spot on top for variable demand, adjusted as usage becomes clearer.

concepts.title: S3 and Object Storage Semantics
concepts.description: S3 stores objects, not files in a directory tree. Understanding that, along with its durability and consistency guarantees and its storage classes, lets you design with S3's model instead of fighting it.
learningObjectives: Explain why S3 is an object store rather than a filesystem, and what that implies for operations like renaming or listing at scale.
Explain S3's durability design and why it is a distinct guarantee from availability.
Explain S3's strong read-after-write consistency model and why older material describes a different, weaker guarantee.
Choose an appropriate storage class for a given access pattern and cost/latency requirement, and describe how a lifecycle policy automates transitions between classes.
Distinguish IAM policies, bucket policies, and Block Public Access as different layers of S3 access control, and explain what each one governs.

sections.heading: Objects, Not Files: What S3 Actually Stores
sections.body:
An S3 **object** is the combination of the data itself (arbitrary bytes, up to 5TB per object), a set of metadata, and a unique **key** -- a string that identifies that object within a **bucket**. That is the whole model: a flat namespace of keys mapped to objects inside a bucket (bucket names are unique across all AWS accounts in a partition), with no directory tree underneath, even though the console shows what looks like nested folders. The console's 'folders' are a display convenience that relies on keys being allowed to contain `/`. A key like `logs/2026/01/app.log` is one string with slashes in it, and the console groups keys by shared prefix to look hierarchical. No folder object is created, moved, or renamed underneath. Two limits are worth knowing: a single PUT can upload at most 5 GB, so larger objects (and, in practice, anything over about 100 MB) should use multipart upload, and S3 supports at least 3,500 write and 5,500 read requests per second per prefix, so request rate scales as you spread keys over more prefixes.

The consequence is that there is no atomic 'rename' of an object, let alone of a 'folder.' Renaming an object means copying it to the new key and deleting the old one: two API calls. Renaming a 'folder' of a million objects that share a prefix means issuing that copy-then-delete pair for each of the million, since nothing renames a prefix in one operation. That is why bulk moves in S3 can be slow and rack up request costs that surprise people the first time they run one on a large prefix. It really is many operations.

sections.heading: Durability vs. Availability: 11 Nines Doesn't Mean What People Assume
sections.body:
S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% durability (eleven nines), a number that is often misread. Durability is about **data loss**: S3 stores each object redundantly across multiple devices in multiple Availability Zones in the Region, so a failed disk, rack, or even AZ essentially never causes an object's bytes to be permanently lost. The figure describes how unlikely permanent loss is over many objects and long periods. It protects against AWS-side loss, not against your own mistakes: an overwrite or delete issued by your code is durably stored too. Enable bucket versioning (optionally with a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions) if you need to recover from accidental overwrites and deletes.

Availability is a separate axis: whether the *service* is reachable and answering requests at a given moment. S3 Standard's design target is lower, 99.99%. The gap matters: a particular GET can fail or time out (a rare availability blip) while the object was never at risk of being lost. Conflating the two leads to an avoidable mistake, assuming that because durability is so strong, retry logic around S3 calls is unnecessary. Code that calls S3 should handle occasional request failures with retries and backoff, because that is governed by availability, not durability.

sections.heading: Consistency: Strong Read-After-Write (and a Bit of History Worth Knowing)
sections.body:
Since a change AWS shipped in December 2020, S3 provides **strong read-after-write consistency** for all operations: a `GET` right after a successful `PUT` returns the latest version, and a list reflects every write that completed before the list request. This sounds like an unremarkable baseline, but the history matters because older blog posts, StackOverflow answers, and defensive application code assume the earlier, weaker model, in which overwrite `PUT`s and `DELETE`s were only eventually consistent, so a read right after a write could briefly return stale or missing data.

That older model caused hard-to-reproduce bugs: write an object, read it back to confirm, and occasionally get a miss or an old version with no error to explain it. You'll still find code with retry loops or artificial delays added to work around it. On modern S3 those workarounds aren't needed for consistency (retries for plain request failures, per the availability discussion, are still worth keeping). Recognize the pattern in older code instead of assuming it still protects against something real.

sections.heading: Storage Classes: Trading Retrieval Speed and Cost for Storage Cost
sections.body:
S3 offers multiple storage classes that trade cheaper per-GB storage against slower retrieval, a per-retrieval fee, or reduced redundancy, and the right choice matches the class to the object's access pattern, not to whichever is cheapest. **S3 Standard** is priced for frequently accessed data with no retrieval fee and millisecond access. **Standard-IA** ('infrequent access') and **One Zone-IA** offer cheaper per-GB storage in exchange for a per-GB retrieval fee -- appropriate for data you access rarely but still need available instantly when you do (One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, so it is lost if that AZ is destroyed and costs less; that is reasonable only for data you can regenerate or that has a copy elsewhere). Both IA classes also have a 30-day minimum storage charge and a 128 KB minimum billable object size. The **Glacier** family (Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval, and Deep Archive) is built for archival data accessed rarely if ever, with per-GB storage costs that are dramatically lower still, in exchange for retrieval times ranging from milliseconds (Instant) to minutes or hours (Flexible: roughly 1-5 minutes expedited, 3-5 hours standard, 5-12 hours bulk) to many hours (Deep Archive, the cheapest tier: within 12 hours standard, 48 hours bulk). Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive objects must be restored to a temporary copy before you can read them, and you pay for the restore. **Intelligent-Tiering** monitors access per object and moves objects between frequent- and infrequent-access tiers for you, a sensible default when you can't predict how a dataset will be accessed over time.

Managing classes by hand doesn't scale, so the standard practice is a **lifecycle policy**: a rule on the bucket (optionally scoped to a key prefix) that transitions objects between classes by age and can expire (delete) them after a set number of days. A common pattern: application logs stay in S3 Standard while recent and likely to be queried, move to Standard-IA after 30 days once queries drop off, move to Glacier after 90 days for cheap retention, and expire after a year once retention requirements are met, without anyone moving an object by hand.

sections.heading: Controlling Access: IAM Policies, Bucket Policies, and Block Public Access
sections.body:
S3 access control has several layers worth naming separately, because an access problem or an accidental exposure can originate in any of them. **IAM identity-based policies**, attached to a user or role, describe what that principal may do in S3 (covered in the IAM concept). **Bucket policies** are resource-based policies attached to the bucket, and they differ in one important way: they can grant access to principals in *other* AWS accounts, or to the public, which an identity-based policy on your own users can't do.
