This is where most 'bucket became public' incidents start: someone writes a bucket policy with an overly broad `Principal` (often `"*"`) meaning to grant one consumer, and it grants everyone. Legacy object and bucket **ACLs** are an older mechanism that AWS recommends keeping disabled in favor of policies, which are more expressive and easier to reason about.

**Block Public Access** is a separate safety mechanism layered on top, configurable per account or per bucket: when enabled, it stops public access from taking effect even if a bucket policy or ACL would grant it. AWS turned it on by default for new buckets (since April 2023) because years of bucket-policy mistakes like the one above caused damaging leaks. Now you must deliberately disable Block Public Access before a public-granting policy can work, which puts a speed bump in front of an easy-to-miss mistake. Separately, new objects are encrypted at rest by default (SSE-S3), so encryption in transit (HTTPS) and the choice of key (SSE-S3 or a KMS key you control, which adds its own key policy as another access layer) are the parts you still decide.

examples.title: Why 'Renaming a Folder' Is Actually Copying Every Object
examples.code:
aws s3 mv s3://reports-bucket/2025-exports/ s3://reports-bucket/archive/2025-exports/ --recursive

# Under the hood, for every single object matching the old prefix, the CLI issues:
#   1. a CopyObject call to the new key
#   2. a DeleteObject call on the old key
# There is no single S3 API call that renames a prefix as one atomic operation.
examples.explanation: This looks like a cheap metadata-only rename, and for a handful of objects it is fast enough that the mechanics don't matter. But S3 has no directory structure, so `2025-exports/` can't be renamed; it is a prefix shared by however many keys match it. The CLI's recursive `mv` loops over every matching key and issues a copy and a delete for each. For a prefix with two million objects, this one command line makes about four million API calls (plus the listing requests), each adding cost and time. That changes how you design large-scale reorganizations: choose key naming schemes up front that you won't need to bulk-rename, instead of assuming a rename is as cheap as on a filesystem.

examples.title: A Lifecycle Policy Automating Storage Class Transitions
examples.explanation: This rule applies only to keys starting with `logs/`, and it encodes how log data is accessed. Recent logs are queried often, so they stay in S3 Standard for 30 days. Query frequency then drops, so the rule moves them to the cheaper Standard-IA class (accepting a small retrieval fee when someone does query month-old logs). At 90 days they move to Glacier, where storage is far cheaper and retrieval takes minutes to hours. At a year, `Expiration` deletes them, assuming the retention requirement has been met by then. None of it needs application code or manual work, and nobody has to remember to do it or leaves a year of logs in the most expensive class because the cleanup never made anyone's task list. Objects under 128 KB are not transitioned by default.

examples.title: A Bucket Policy That Accidentally Makes Everything Public
examples.explanation: The `Sid`, 'AllowPartnerRead', shows the intent: grant one business partner read access to exported files. But `"Principal": "*"` doesn't mean 'the partner'. It means any caller on the internet, so every object in the bucket is downloadable by anyone who has or guesses a key. The fixed version names a specific AWS account (`111122223333`, a placeholder), which limits the grant to principals from that account. (`:root` here means the account as a whole; that account's admins still have to delegate access to their own users and roles.) Writing `"*"` when you meant 'one known external party' is the class of error Block Public Access catches: with it enabled on the account or bucket, the broad policy would not grant the public access it appears to, even though the document is valid.

misconceptions.description: S3 has real folders and directories, so listing or renaming 'a folder' is a cheap, near-instant operation regardless of how many objects it contains.
misconceptions.clarification: S3 has a flat key namespace inside each bucket; what the console displays as folders is a rendering convenience based on shared key prefixes containing `/` characters, not an actual directory structure. Listing by prefix filters keys rather than doing a directory lookup, and there is no atomic rename: 'renaming a folder' is a copy-then-delete for every object sharing that prefix, which can be slow and costly at scale.
misconceptions.fact: S3 has a flat key namespace inside each bucket; what the console displays as folders is a rendering convenience based on shared key prefixes containing `/` characters, not an actual directory structure.

misconceptions.description: S3's 'eleven nines of durability' means requests to S3 will essentially never fail.
misconceptions.clarification: Durability (essentially never permanently losing stored data, thanks to redundant storage across devices and AZs) and availability (the service answering a given request successfully, designed for 99.99% for S3 Standard) are different guarantees. A request can fail or time out, which the availability figure governs, even though the object data was never at risk. Application code calling S3 should still retry transient failures, however high durability is.

exercises.prompt: An application 'reorganizes' its S3 data nightly by moving all objects under a date-based prefix containing several million keys to a new archive prefix, using a naive per-object copy-then-delete loop in application code. The job has started timing out and its S3 request costs have spiked noticeably. Diagnose why this approach doesn't scale and propose a better strategy.
exercises.code:
# pseudocode for the current nightly job
for key in list_all_objects_under_prefix("data/2026-01-14/"):
    copy_object(from=key, to=key.replace("data/2026-01-14/", "archive/2026-01-14/"))
    delete_object(key)
# runs once per object, sequentially, for several million objects
hints: Recall that S3 has no atomic rename or move for a prefix. What does that imply about the number of API calls this loop makes?
The loop processes objects one at a time, sequentially -- is there a way to make many of these copy/delete operations happen concurrently instead of strictly one after another?
Consider whether copying every object is necessary at all, or whether a different key naming scheme avoids bulk moves, and what managed S3 feature can run a copy over a manifest of millions of keys.
exercises.solutionCode:
# Better: avoid needing a bulk move at all by naming keys with the archive
# destination baked in from the start, OR at minimum parallelize the work instead
# of running it one object at a time: create an S3 Batch Operations job whose
# manifest lists the keys and whose operation is Copy into the archive prefix
# (concurrency, retries and progress reports are built in), then remove the
# originals with a lifecycle Expiration rule scoped to the old prefix.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The job makes two API calls (copy and delete) per object, sequentially, for several million objects. A sequential loop can't be made fast, and S3 has no bulk-rename primitive to fall back on, so the per-object cost is inherent. The more scalable fix is S3 Batch Operations, a managed feature for this kind of job: given a manifest of keys, it runs an operation such as Copy across all of them with parallelism, retries, and progress tracking, so your code doesn't manage a slow loop. Batch Operations copies; it doesn't delete the originals as part of the same job, so remove them with a lifecycle Expiration rule on the old prefix or a second job. Better still, avoid the bulk move: write new data under its eventual archive-style key structure from the start. A design that assumes prefixes can be cheaply restructured later is fighting the object-store model.

exercises.prompt: Write an S3 lifecycle rule (JSON) for objects under the 'backups/' prefix: keep them in S3 Standard for the first 14 days (frequent restore testing happens in this window), move them to Standard-IA after that, and permanently delete them after 180 days. Restores after day 180 are never needed.
hints: A Transition entry's 'Days' value is the object age at which the transition happens. You don't need a rule for the initial Standard period, since that is the default state before any transition fires.
Only one transition is needed, since only two storage classes are involved (Standard, implicitly, then Standard-IA). Don't add a Glacier transition that wasn't asked for.
Expiration works like Transitions: a Days value after which the object is deleted instead of moved.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Objects need no rule for their first 14 days, since S3 Standard is where every object starts. The single `Transitions` entry with `"Days": 14` moves objects to `STANDARD_IA` at that age, so restore testing in the first 14 days finds them in Standard with no retrieval fee, while older backups move to cheaper storage. `Expiration` at 180 days deletes the object, matching the stated fact that nothing past day 180 is restored. A Glacier tier would be over-engineering: two access-pattern phases need one transition and one expiration. Two caveats: Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum storage charge (harmless here, since objects stay in IA for 166 days), and older AWS documentation required objects to be 30 days old before a Standard-IA transition, so confirm your S3 configuration accepts a 14-day transition before relying on it.

assessments.prompt: A team observes that an S3 GET request occasionally fails with a transient error, even though they're confident their object was never lost or corrupted. Which statement best explains this?
options: This should be impossible; S3's eleven-nines durability guarantee means requests essentially never fail.

Durability (data not being lost) and availability (the service successfully responding to a given request) are different guarantees; S3's availability target is lower than its durability figure, so occasional transient request failures are expected and should be handled with retry logic.
This is only possible if the bucket's lifecycle policy has an error in it.
This indicates the object was stored in a One Zone-IA storage class, which is the only class where transient failures can occur.
assessments.explanation: Durability and availability are separate guarantees: durability is about not losing the data over time (S3 Standard's eleven nines), while availability is about the service answering a given request right now (designed for 99.99% for S3 Standard, far fewer nines). An occasional request failure is consistent with the availability figure and doesn't contradict durability, which is why the premise of the “This should be impossible; S3's eleven-nines durability…” option -- treating durability as if it covered request success, is wrong. The “This indicates the object was stored…” option incorrectly ties this to a specific storage class (transient request failures aren't a One Zone-IA-specific phenomenon), and the “This is only possible if the bucket's…” option introduces an unrelated cause (lifecycle policies affect storage class transitions and expiration, not the success rate of GET requests).

assessments.prompt: A developer expects `aws s3 mv s3://bucket/old-prefix/ s3://bucket/new-prefix/ --recursive` on a prefix containing 500,000 objects to complete almost instantly, the way renaming a folder does on a local filesystem. Why is that expectation wrong?
options: The command will in fact complete instantly, because S3 secretly maintains a hidden directory tree beneath what the console displays.
The AWS CLI doesn't actually support recursive moves, so this specific command will fail outright.

S3 has no atomic rename operation for a prefix; because S3 is a flat key-value namespace rather than a real directory tree, the CLI must issue an individual CopyObject followed by a DeleteObject for every one of the 500,000 objects -- hundreds of thousands of separate API calls, not one instant metadata change.
The delay only occurs if Block Public Access happens to be enabled on the bucket.
assessments.explanation: S3 is a flat namespace of keys within a bucket: a folder is only a shared key prefix, with no directory object to rename in one operation. The CLI's recursive move is a copy-then-delete loop over every matching key, so a 500,000-object prefix becomes roughly a million API calls, each with its own latency and cost. That is inherent to the model, not a CLI inefficiency. The “The AWS CLI doesn't actually support recursive…” option is factually wrong (recursive move is supported and will run, just slowly and at real cost), the “The command will in fact complete instantly…” option invents a hidden directory structure that doesn't exist, and the “The delay only occurs if Block Public…” option introduces Block Public Access, which governs public access grants and has nothing to do with copy/delete latency.

assessments.prompt: While reviewing an older codebase, you find application code that, after every S3 PUT, sleeps briefly and retries a GET in a loop until the new data appears, with a comment saying 'S3 needs a moment to catch up.' What's the most accurate assessment of this code today?
options: It's still necessary -- S3 has always been eventually consistent for all operations and always will be.
It's actually a workaround for IAM policy propagation delay, unrelated to S3's own consistency model.
It indicates the bucket must be using the One Zone-IA storage class, the only class with eventual consistency.

It was a legitimate workaround for S3's pre-December-2020 weaker consistency model for overwrite PUTs and deletes, but on modern S3 -- which provides strong read-after-write consistency for all operations -- it's no longer needed for consistency reasons, though general retry logic for transient request failures can still be worthwhile.
assessments.explanation: Before December 2020, S3 had a weaker model in which overwrite PUTs and deletes could briefly leave a read returning stale or missing data, which is what this sleep-and-retry code worked around. Since then, S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all operations, so a GET right after a successful PUT reflects the latest write and the concern this code guards against is gone. The “It's still necessary -- S3 has always…” option misstates S3's current guarantee, the “It indicates the bucket must be using…” option ties the behavior to a storage class that has nothing to do with read-after-write consistency, and the “It's actually a workaround for IAM policy…” option introduces IAM propagation, an unrelated AWS behavior entirely separate from S3's own object consistency model. Note that generic retry logic for transient request failures, governed by availability rather than consistency, can still be reasonable to keep -- just not for this stated reason.

assessments.prompt: A colleague proposes storing every uploaded file in S3 Glacier Deep Archive from the moment it's uploaded, reasoning that it's the cheapest storage class and therefore the best default. Explain what's wrong with this reasoning and how you'd actually choose a storage class and lifecycle strategy for a typical file-upload feature.
assessments.modelAnswer: The flaw is treating cheapest per-GB storage as the only variable, when storage classes trade that cost against retrieval speed and, for the infrequent-access and archive tiers, a per-retrieval fee. Deep Archive is cheapest because retrieving an object can take many hours, which is unacceptable for a typical upload feature where users expect to view or download a file within seconds, not request a restore and wait. Choose a class from the access pattern of the data (and the object sizes: the IA classes bill a 128 KB minimum per object, so millions of tiny files are a poor fit): new uploads are accessed often right after upload (reviewed, shared, followed up), so they belong in S3 Standard, with no retrieval fee and instant access. As files age, access usually drops off predictably, which is what a lifecycle policy should automate: transition objects to Standard-IA after some observed window of low access (say, 30-60 days, tuned to the actual product's usage data), and move to Glacier-tier storage only files that are effectively archival, if that applies to this feature at all. If per-file access is hard to predict (some files stay hot for months, others go cold in days), S3 Intelligent-Tiering is a reasonable alternative to a fixed age-based rule, since it tracks each object's access and moves it between tiers automatically. The principle: design the strategy around when and how fast the data must be retrievable, and use cost as the tiebreaker among options that meet that requirement.
